summaries.Q914013: Shaped like a long ship's hull, this rock in Biarritz, between the Port-Vieux and the Port des pêcheurs, carries a statue of the Virgin blessed in 1865, which commemorates the return of Biarritz whalers caught in a storm in 1864. A metal footbridge designed from 1886 to 1887, wrongly credited to the Eiffel works, leads to it.
summaries.Q3378183: Standing at the pointe Saint-Martin, in Biarritz, on a rocky bluff above the Bay of Biscay, it has guided sailors since 1 February 1834. 47 metres high, it carries a Fresnel lens optic installed in 1904, with a range of 26 nautical miles. Its stairway has 248 steps and its copper dome twelve bronze lion heads.
summaries.Q12254690: Designed by Vauban in 1680 and built in the late 17th century at the request of Louis XIV, it occupies a hill in Bayonne overlooking the Saint-Esprit district. Its square, 480 metres on each side, carries four bastions with orillons. A prison under the Revolution and the First Empire, then a military camp, it has housed the 1er RPIMa since 1960.
summaries.Q22980085: On this square in Bayonne stood a fortified work designed by Vauban in 1680 and built in the late 17th century at the request of Louis XIV. The stronghold was decommissioned in 1907 and the porte de France taken down. The bartizan, which collapsed into the Adour in 1937, was restored in 2006; the remains were listed as historic monuments in 2013.
summaries.Q22920587: A 19th century military building, this riding hall in Bayonne was built in 1825 to plans by the engineer colonel Emy. It has been listed as a historic monument since 17 September 1943.
summaries.Q2866138: Opened in 1893 in Bayonne, this neo-Moorish bullring is the largest in the South-West, with more than 10,000 seats. The banker Albin Salzedo had launched the project in 1891 through public subscription. After the arson fire of 1919, the upper part, originally of wood, was rebuilt in concrete.
summaries.Q3411513: At 1 bis place Clemenceau, in Biarritz, this shop keeps an interior decoration of mosaics and stucco dating from the late 19th century. That decoration is listed as a historic monument by an order of 1 October 2006.
summaries.Q3065485: Laid out in Bayonne between 1987 and 1990 on a bastion of Vauban's fortifications overlooking the war memorial, this 3,000 m2 municipal garden is designed in a Japanese manner, with a pond and a waterfall. It brings together nearly a thousand taxa in nine sections. Admission is free, Tuesday to Saturday, from mid-April to mid-October.
summaries.Q12254687: In the Saint-Étienne district, north of Bayonne, this Jewish cemetery covers two hectares and keeps nearly three thousand graves dating from the 17th to the 19th century. A mortuary house shaped like an ancient temple was opened there in 1862. The site was the scene of a battle in 1814, during the siege of Bayonne.
summaries.Q29015536: This disused Cistercian nunnery stands in Bayonne, on the right bank of the Adour estuary. The nuns settled on the site in 1245 and the abbey closed in 1790. The siege of Bayonne damaged a large part of the buildings; the site was turned into a factory in the 19th century. What remains was converted into housing in 2008.
summaries.Q3344734: This convent in Anglet, at 102 avenue de Montbrun, was founded by Blessed Louis-Édouard Cestac for the congregation of the Servants of Mary. Cestac bought the Châteauneuf farming estate in 1838 and the first community settled there in 1842. The present chapel, to plans by M. Bourdenne, was consecrated in 1886 by Mgr Ducellier.
summaries.Q2967845: This private house in Biarritz was designed in the eclectic style by Joseph Louis Duc, one of the architects of the Palais de Justice in Paris, for Charles Boulart. On Duc's death in 1879, François Roux carried on the work until 1881. The facades and the roof have been listed as historic monuments since 1975.
summaries.Q1736171: Gothic, it overlooks the Adour and the Nive from a rise in the historic quarter of Bayonne and is the episcopal seat of the diocese. Its two spires were finished in the 19th century. A cloister, one of the largest in France, adjoins it to the south. It has been on the World Heritage List since 1998, as part of the routes of Santiago de Compostela.
summaries.Q2620702: The musée des Beaux-Arts de Bayonne, in Petit Bayonne, keeps a large number of works by the painters Léon Bonnat and Paul César Helleu. Closed on 11 April 2011, it reopened on 27 November 2025. The building, raised after the fire that ravaged the town hall in December 1889 and opened in 1901, has been wholly devoted to it since 1976.
summaries.Q1460236: This Bayonne stadium is the home ground of Aviron bayonnais. Opened on 21 September 1935 under the name stade Saint-Léon, it was at first a velodrome stadium and hosted the finish of several Tour de France stages. In the early 2000s it took the name of Jean Dauger, a club player who died in 1999, whose bronze statue stands at the entrance.
summaries.Q2680279: This château in Bayonne was built in the early 18th century by Marie-Anne de Neubourg, exiled queen of Spain, who never really lived in it. Napoleon I bought it in 1808 and made it one of his imperial palaces; the abdication of the Spanish Bourbons was signed there. Ravaged by fire in 1825, it is in ruins and has been under renovation since 2012.
summaries.Q2385374: Opened in 1904 on rue Pellot in Biarritz, an annexe of the synagogue of Bayonne, it was raised to plans by the Bayonne architect Charles Pasquier, who died before they were carried out. Its Holy Ark comes from the synagogue of Peyrehorade. Closed to worship in 1995 for safety reasons, it partly reopened in the summer of 2012.
summaries.Q3508031: Built in 1836-1837 at 35 rue Maubec, in the Saint-Esprit district north of Bayonne, it stands back from the street, on a courtyard, behind a gate flanked by two pavilions; its facade is neoclassical. Unusually, its entrance faces east, the Holy Ark against the west wall. It has been classified as a historic monument since 20 January 2012.
summaries.Q2041472: This Orthodox place of worship of the Russian tradition stands at 8 avenue de l'Impératrice in Biarritz, dedicated to Saint Alexander Nevsky and to the Protection of the Mother of God. Decided in 1879 for the Russian holiday community, the church was built to a design by Nikolai Nikonov with the Gers architect Oscar Tisnès and consecrated in 1892.
summaries.Q1165840: Home of Biarritz olympique Pays basque, a rugby union club, this Biarritz sports park can hold 13,400 spectators. The land was acquired by the town in 1906. The park is named after a former owner, José Aguilera y Chapin. The main stand is from 1922, the tribune Coubertin from 1963. Since 2025 the pitch has been synthetic.
summaries.Q2389536: The former musée de la Mer, in Biarritz facing the rocher de la Vierge, is an Art Deco building set against the cliff of the Atalaye plateau, opened in 1933. An extension completed in 2011 doubled the visiting area and increased the number of tanks, at the cost of the stuffed bird room, removed. A jellyfish space opened in 2025.
summaries.Q12258310: This medieval fortress in Bayonne, raised from the late 11th century by the viscounts of Labourd on the edge of a Roman castrum, rests on three reinforced Roman towers. It took this name in the late 15th century, a new castle having been built in Petit-Bayonne. The north-west strongpoint of Vauban's fortifications, it has lost its keep.
summaries.Q3146296: Raised in Biarritz in 1854-1855 as the summer residence of Napoleon III and Eugénie de Montijo, under the name villa Eugénie, the building became a hotel-casino after the sale of 1881, then the hôtel du Palais. Burnt in February 1903, it was rebuilt by Édouard-Jean Niermans, who made it a luxury hotel.
summaries.Q17486224: Raised in the Petit Bayonne district, in Bayonne, between 1856 and 1869 by Hippolyte Durand and Hippolyte Guichenné, this neo-Gothic church owes most of its funding to the bequest of the banker Jacques-Taurin de Lormand. Its spires, too heavy, were demolished in 1901 and replaced in 1903 by the two present belfry towers.
summaries.Q3329506: Housed since 1924 on the quai des Corsaires in Bayonne, in the maison Dagourette, a bourgeois residence of the late 16th century, it holds the largest ethnographic collection devoted to the Basque Country in France. Since the 2001 renovation, the permanent display occupies three floors and shows 3,000 objects in 20 themed rooms.
summaries.Q2941116: This Art Deco building was put up in 1929 by the architect Alfred Laulhé, on the Grande Plage in Biarritz. Besides gaming rooms and reception rooms, it holds a theatre, a swimming pool and a restaurant, and it is run by the Groupe Barrière. The entrance hall, the gallery and the elevation have been protected as historic monuments since 1992.
summaries.Q3585022: This neo-Gothic church of grey stone overlooks the Port Vieux, in Biarritz. Its construction lasted from 1898 to 1903, on the site of an earlier chapel. Placed under the patronage of Saint Eugenia, patron saint of Empress Eugénie de Montijo, it keeps stained glass windows by Luc-Olivier Merson.
summaries.Q12254685: Built from 1837 to 1842 by Nicolas Vionnois, place de la Liberté in Bayonne, this perfect square 50 metres on each side holds the town hall and the théâtre Michel-Portal. Its pediment bears six allegories of the town's activities, remade in cast iron after the fire of 1889. Rebuilt in the Italian manner from 2004 to 2006, the auditorium seats 592.
summaries.Q20978463: An oratory was first opened in Biarritz in the basement of the Thermes salins, for spa patients, some of whom could not reach the parish of Saint-Martin, too far off. This neo-Romanesque church is under the patronage of Saint Charles Borromeo; its foundation stone was blessed on 28 August 1898. The stained glass is by the glassmaker Mauméjean.
summaries.Q20972906: Consecrated in 1895 in Biarritz, this Catholic church served as the chapel of the adjoining Dominican convent, whose memory is kept by the cloister and the choir stalls. Two mosaics by the Facchina firm of Paris frame the choir. The stained glass, lost in the bombing of 27 March 1944, was remade after the war.
summaries.Q3582683: Saint Martin is the patron saint of Biarritz; the parish that bears his name goes back to the time of English rule. Romanesque in style, the church was enlarged and altered in 1541, according to a date borne on a pillar, then restored from 1861. It was the parish church of the commune until 1894.
summaries.Q12268877: On the rocky coast of Biarritz, this neo-medieval villa was built for Ange Du Fresnay by the architect Alphonse Bertrand; the keep and the pepperpot turret are by Dominique Morin, in 1889. Its name pays tribute to the owner's wife, Marie Belza Dubreuil. A Russian restaurant in 1923, burnt in 1974, it holds flats.
summaries.Q12257267: This Catholic church stands in the Saint-Esprit district, in Bayonne, opposite the SNCF station. In 1463 Louis XI had a new church built to replace the Romanesque chapel of the priory; once a collegiate church, it acquired Flamboyant Gothic vaults. Enlarged in the late 19th century, it was listed as a historic monument in 2008.
summaries.Q15940485: A former wine estate turned into a country house, it stands chemin de Laharie, in Bayonne. After the fierce fighting of the siege of Bayonne in 1814, the house was restored in 1848, then altered by the architect Gomez in 1918. The château, its railing and its entrance gate have been listed as historic monuments since 2009.
summaries.Q17486123: This iron bridge over the Adour, in Bayonne, was also called pont de Mousserolles, after a district. Ordered in 1864 from the Daney works in Bordeaux, 270 metres long and 14 metres wide, it rested on eight piers of cast iron and cement and carried two railway tracks. Replaced by the pont Charles-Vaillant, it was largely demolished.
summaries.Q2957492: Built from 1864 to 1866 at the request of Eugénie de Montijo, wife of Napoleon III, it is the work of Émile Boeswillwald and blends the Romanesque-Byzantine and Hispano-Moorish styles. Dedicated to the Mexican black virgin Our Lady of Guadalupe, avenue de la Marne in Biarritz, it is the town's only built trace of the imperial holidays.
summaries.Q29912862: This Catholic church in Anglet keeps galleries and balustrades of the 17th and 18th centuries. Its organ dates from 1912.
summaries.Q65561979: Dating from the 19th century, it is one of the oldest villas in Biarritz. Bought in 1921 by Prince Alexander of Oldenburg, who lived there until his death, it was turned into a residential building after the Second World War, while its 7 hectare grounds were divided into plots and sold.
summaries.Q65570571: Opened at the very end of the 19th century, this municipal cemetery in Biarritz has its main entrance on avenue du Sabaou and has a chapel. The graves there are modest. It holds a French military plot and a British plot, as well as the graves of four Swedish sailors who died in the wreck of the Padosa, in December 1907.
summaries.Q3145631: Built in 1928 in Biarritz by the architects Louis-Hippolyte Boileau and Paul Perrotte, this luxury hotel is one of the legacies of the town's Roaring Twenties and has kept its furniture through three renovations. Its facades, its roofs, its staircases and some galleries have been listed as historic monuments since 1990.
summaries.Q3450333: In the Grand Bayonne district, this street owes its name to the butchers' guild, present there since at least the 13th century. It then bore the Gascon name Carnaceirie, was called “rue de la Boucherie” in 1314 and took its present name in 1716.
summaries.Q3451989: In the Grand Bayonne district, this street runs from the rue Montaut, by the cloister, to the boulevard du Rempart Lachepaillet, near the cathedral. Its name refers to the prebendaries, those who receive a prebend; its former name was rue des Prébendiers. It appears on the 1612 map of Bayonne.
summaries.Q24083161: A former Catholic chapel in Bayonne's historic quarter, it opens onto rue Douer and runs along place Montaut, near the cathedral. It was built in 1860 in neo-Romanesque style, with a single nave and no transept, at the request of Father de Quevedo. Deconsecrated in 1981, it serves as a multipurpose hall for the coeducational collège Notre-Dame.
summaries.Q52726969: A small stony cemetery with few trees, it lies avenue du 14-avril-1814, in the Saint-Étienne district of Bayonne, in the shade of the église Saint-Étienne-lès-Bayonne. Its gravel paths cross at right angles and there are no funerary chapels. The painters Émile Betsellère and Léon Bonnat are buried there.
summaries.Q17484909: This arched bridge crosses the Adour in Bayonne and links the town centre to the Saint-Esprit district. 200 metres long, it has 7 arches. A first bridge, of wood, had been built around 1150. The present structure was begun in 1846 and finished in 1849, then widened in 1910 to let the tramway through.
summaries.Q2948420: This is the last stretch of the Côte d'Argent, which ends at Anglet: the sands of the Landes meet heavily eroded rock strata there, before the pointe Saint-Martin and the phare de Biarritz. The name of this hamlet is said to come from lovers caught by the tide; Paul Raymond derives it from a cave at sea level.
summaries.Q22703880: In Anglet, the church was built to plans by Pierre Fonterme under the direction of Charles Hébrard; the foundation stone was blessed in 1930 and the dedication took place in 1932. The interior, in Labourdin Basque style in the Art Deco manner, has two tiers of galleries, frescoes by Berthe Grimard in the choir and two Mauméjean mosaics of 1938.
summaries.Q31187878: In Anglet, on the edge of the golf de Chiberta, this villa covered in pink cement combines round arches and a neo-Gothic corner tower. Built between 1927 and 1930 by the Gélos architect brothers for the American Robert Poole, it was the first built along the course. Its name comes from the island of Prinkipo, off Istanbul.
summaries.Q56417738: This multi-sport stadium in Anglet, opened on 20 January 1935, was first the ground of the rugby league club Côte basque XIII. Aviron bayonnais was hosted there in 1940, then moved for good to the stade Saint-Léon in 1941. Since then it has served Anglet ORC, a rugby union club, and a few matches of the Genêts d'Anglet, in football.
summaries.Q134407429: Rebuilt in 1866 in Biarritz by Jules Labat, who was mayor of Bayonne, under the direction of the architect Alphonse Bertrand, it stands very close to the château Boulart and the église Saint-Martin. Its hall holds the portraits of Jules and Gabrielle Labat by Léon Bonnat. Restructured in the 1980s, it now contains flats.
summaries.Q3558686: This neo-Basque house of the early 20th century stands at 110 rue d'Espagne in Biarritz, raised under the supervision of the architects Henri Sauvage and Charles Sarazin for the stockbroker Albert-Guillaume Leuba. The town of Biarritz has owned it since 1978; the villa holds the cultural services and its garden is now public.
summaries.Q24577284: A street of the Grand Bayonne district, below the cathedral, it runs from the carrefour des Cinq-Cantons to the rue Poissonnerie. The origin of its name remains uncertain: it may come from salida, “exit”, from the name of an old and powerful Bayonne family of the Middle Ages, or from the salt brought there by boat.
summaries.Q3449378: A Bayonne street in the Grand Bayonne district, it links la Plachotte to the rue d'Espagne and runs along the place des Victoires, of which it is the only public access. Houses there back onto the old wall of the Roman town. The origin of its name is unknown; old deeds also call it rue des Pitarrers, after cider merchants.
summaries.Q3450001: This street was the main artery of the Saint-Esprit district in Bayonne, founded by the Jewish community; the people of Bayonne called it “rue la Juiverie”. It begins at place de la République and ends at boulevard Jean-d'Amou. Some campaign to name it after the anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss, whose grandfather was rabbi of Bayonne.
summaries.Q41794196: In Labourdin style, this church of Saint-Pierre-d'Irube is dedicated to the apostle Peter. Its building date is uncertain: a resolution of the Bayonne town council of 2 October 1482 proves that a church existed then. It is not listed as a historic monument; its benoîterie is the only classified building in the commune.
summaries.Q111211325: Set on the cliffs of Biarritz, between the lighthouse and the golf course, this Belle Époque luxury hotel was completed in 1907 and received the world's elite, among them Queen Amélie of Portugal and King Edward VII. Requisitioned by German troops during the Second World War, it was bought in June 2022 by the Experimental group.
summaries.Q3450514: In the Grand Bayonne district, this street links the porte d'Espagne, to the south, to the place Louis-Pasteur, to the north, and owes its name to the nearness of that gate. It brings together two old sections, the rue des Tendes and the rue Mayou, and took its present name only in the late 19th century. It was pedestrianised and paved in 2007.
